<a id="pm-h-95"></a>
#### Transfer of the correlation polynomial

Fix $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$ and compact $K\subset\mathcal D_k$. Choose $0<r<d_K/1000$. Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:rr-nails" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:rr-nails">70</a> and, for each endpoint, select an indexed nail close to it. For all small enough meshes both corresponding nails lie within $r/2$ of that endpoint. Nails selected for endpoints in distinct slots are distinct. In both samples discard the event that a loop of diameter at least $d_K/4$ comes within $r$ of an endpoint. Lemma <a href="#lem:rr-estimates" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:rr-estimates">69</a> bounds the probability of these exceptions by $C_K(r/d_K)^\gamma+o(1)$, uniformly for the individual tuples in $K$.

On the remaining event, a relevant loop $L$ surrounds the nails near one endpoint of each of two distinct slots, and excludes a nail near the other endpoint of a separated slot. It is therefore non-trivial in the exact sense of Lemma <a href="#lem:rr-nails" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:rr-nails">70</a>, so $\psi(L)$ is defined. For those two slots the winding differences at the corresponding nails are nonzero by <a href="#eq:rr-winding-difference" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-winding-difference">[eq:rr-winding-difference]</a>. Thus $\psi(L)$ separates each of the two nail pairs. In particular, it encloses one nail from each of two distinct slots, whose distance is at least $d_K-O(r+\delta)$. This proves that $\psi(L)$ itself has diameter at least $d_K/4$. Its endpoint-avoidance event is consequently applicable; smallness of the partner has not been assumed away.

Endpoint indicators and nearby-nail indicators agree for both loops. Equation <a href="#eq:rr-winding-difference" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-winding-difference">[eq:rr-winding-difference]</a> now gives, for *every* slot, <a id="eq:rr-signature"></a>$$D_i(\psi(L))=\frac{s_L}{s_{\psi(L)}}D_i(L).
 \label{eq:rr-signature}$$ The inverse bijection gives the same statement starting with a relevant loop in the second sample. Hence it is a bijection between all relevant loops, preserving their entire separation vectors up to one sign per loop. For a block $B$ in an even partition, $$\prod_{i\in B}D_i(\psi(L))
    =\left(\frac{s_L}{s_{\psi(L)}}\right)^{|B|}
                       \prod_{i\in B}D_i(L)
    =\prod_{i\in B}D_i(L).$$ Transporting the injective labels in <a href="#eq:rr-even-polynomial" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-even-polynomial">[eq:rr-even-polynomial]</a> therefore makes the two polynomials *exactly equal* on the good event. This uses the actual bijection, so distinct loops are never identified with one another. Cauchy–Schwarz and <a href="#eq:rr-UI" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-UI">[eq:rr-UI]</a> bound the expectation error by $C_K(r/d_K)^{\gamma/2}+o(1)$.

<a id="eq:rr-isoradial-transfer"></a>
It remains to pass from the auxiliary mixed samples to the intended homogeneous ones. Fix $R>10M$ and couple their restrictions identically in $B(0,R)$ using the local-law assertion of Lemma <a href="#lem:rr-nails" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:rr-nails">70</a>; for small enough mesh this disk lies in both homogeneous windows. Off the escaping-loop event in either sample, all relevant complete loops are identical. Equations <a href="#eq:rr-escape" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-escape">[eq:rr-escape]</a> and <a href="#eq:rr-UI" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-UI">[eq:rr-UI]</a> bound the expectation error by $C_K(M/R)^{\gamma/2}$. Let the mesh tend to zero, then $r\downarrow0$ and $R\uparrow\infty$. Writing $\Phi^{\alpha}_{k,\delta}$ for the fair-signed correlation on $\delta\mathbb L(\alpha)$, we obtain $$\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\sup_{\boldsymbol u\in K}
 \left|\Phi^{\pi/2}_{k,\delta}(\boldsymbol u)
                   -\Phi^{\alpha}_{k,\delta}(\boldsymbol u)\right|=0.
 \label{eq:rr-isoradial-transfer}$$ No diameter threshold needs to be a continuity point: all small loops were removed by the even-moment identity itself.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-rr-nails-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-rr-nails</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:rr-rotation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:rr-rotation">67</a>.* The rectangular model on $\mathbb L(\alpha)$ is invariant under reflection $S_{\alpha/2}$ about $e^{i\alpha/2}\mathbb R$ (Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Krachun, et al. 2026, Remark 1.8) <a id="pm-cite-55"></a>[[DCKKMO2026Rotation](#ref-DCKKMO2026Rotation)]. Its fair-sign height correlations inherit that symmetry. If the chosen endpoint rounding is not reflection equivariant, the reflected representatives differ by $O(\delta)$, which is harmless by <a href="#eq:rr-continuity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-continuity">[eq:rr-continuity]</a>. Apply <a href="#eq:rr-isoradial-transfer" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-isoradial-transfer">[eq:rr-isoradial-transfer]</a> at the original and reflected tuples. The square model is consequently asymptotically invariant under $S_{\alpha/2}$, uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathcal D_k$. Composing with its exact horizontal-reflection symmetry yields invariance under rotation through $\alpha$. Square symmetries cover the endpoints and the other half of the circle. This proves the assertion for each fixed rotation.

The estimate <a href="#eq:rr-continuity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-continuity">[eq:rr-continuity]</a> upgrades this to uniformity in the rotation angle. Indeed, the orthogonal images of $K$ form a compact subset of $\mathcal D_k$, and a finite angular net approximates every rotation with endpoint displacement at most $C_K$ times its angular mesh. First use convergence at the finitely many net angles, and then let the angular mesh decrease. Reflections follow by composition with an exact square symmetry. This argument requires no estimate uniform in a degenerating isoradial angle.

Finally, any translation differs from a period translation of the mesh-$\delta$ square lattice by a vector of length $O(\delta)$. Exact period invariance and the location-uniform estimate <a href="#eq:rr-continuity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-continuity">[eq:rr-continuity]</a> handle this residual displacement, uniformly over *all* translation vectors. Every plane isometry is a translation followed by an orthogonal map. The fixed rotation and dilation identifying $\mathbb L(\pi/2)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ merely change the mesh convention and compact set. These observations prove <a href="#eq:rr-target" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:rr-target">[eq:rr-target]</a> for the original square lattice. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-96"></a>
#### The whole-plane field input

<a id="stmt-cor-rr-gff-input"></a>
<div id="cor:rr-gff-input" class="corollary">

**Corollary 71** (The endpoint whole-plane field limit). *The fair unit-jump plane height of critical square-lattice $\operatorname{FK}_4$ converges on neutral smooth compactly supported tests to $\sqrt{2/\pi}$ times the whole-plane GFF with Green kernel $G(x,y)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x-y|$. In particular, Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a> holds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cor-rr-gff-input"><summary>Proof of stmt-cor-rr-gff-input</summary>

*Proof.* Lemma <a href="#lem:rr-bkw" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:rr-bkw">68</a> identifies the discrete gradient law with the isotropic six-vertex law at $(\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c)
=(1,1,2)$. Theorem <a href="#thm:rr-rotation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:rr-rotation">67</a> gives precisely the compact-$\mathcal D_k$, all-isometries symmetry statement used as Theorem 4.1 in (Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers, et al. 2026) <a id="pm-cite-56"></a>[[SixVertexGFF2026](#ref-SixVertexGFF2026)], at this parameter. We may therefore apply its isotropic Theorem 2.8, using the remaining spectral, regularity, and free-energy results cited and proved there. The passage from correlations to smooth field tests is part of its Section 8. No anisotropic extension or general-parameter loop-functional assertion is needed here.

At $\mathbf c=2$ one has $\Delta=-1$, so the variance multiplier in that theorem is $2/\arccos(-1)=2/\pi$. A fixed rotation and dilation of the lattice does not change the neutral whole-plane Green quadratic form: the dilation adds a constant to the logarithmic kernel and each test has integral zero. For every real $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $\int\rho=0$, the convergence therefore gives $$\mathbb E e^{i\langle h_\delta,\rho\rangle}
 \longrightarrow
 \exp\left\{-\frac1\pi
       \iint \rho(x)G(x,y)\rho(y)\,dx\,dy\right\}.$$ Apply the same assertion to every real linear combination of a finite family of neutral tests to obtain joint convergence. This is exactly Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:q4tools"></a>
### The endpoint field and a four-arm estimate

Throughout this section and the next, $q=4$ and $p=p_c=2/3$. We use the critical isotropic square-lattice law, with mesh $\delta$. The medial loop weight is $2$. Resolve each contact inside a disk of radius less than $\delta/100$, preserving the prescribed pairing, so that the lattice loops are disjoint simple curves. These resolutions change uniform curve distance by $O(\delta)$ and do not cross an actual open primal or dual edge. Orient each strand by the convention that primal vertices lie on its left. Independently for each loop, choose with equal probabilities this orientation or its reverse. The resulting height has jumps of size one. In the plane it is defined modulo a constant; its pairing with a smooth compactly supported density of integral zero is well defined.

We fix the normalization <a id="q4field:normalization"></a>$$\label{q4field:normalization}
 G_{\mathbb C}(x,y)=-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log|x-y|,
 \qquad \sigma^2=\frac{2}{\pi},
 \qquad \lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}},
 \qquad 2\sigma\lambda_0=1.$$ Thus $\Phi_V$ will denote the Dirichlet free field whose covariance is the Green operator for $-\Delta$ on $V$.

<a id="stmt-q4field-height-comparison"></a>
<div id="q4field:height-comparison" class="lemma">

<a id="q4field:height-comparison-L2"></a>
**Lemma 72** (Comparison of height conventions). *Couple the cellwise lattice height $h_\delta^{\mathrm{cell}}$ and the height $h_\delta^{\mathrm{geom}}$ defined by the smoothed loop interiors using the same independent loop signs. For every smooth compactly supported neutral density $\rho$, $$\label{q4field:height-comparison-L2}
 \mathbb E\left|
   \langle h_\delta^{\mathrm{geom}}
          -h_\delta^{\mathrm{cell}},\rho\rangle\right|^2
 \longrightarrow0.$$ This conclusion uses only bulk crossing and passage-count estimates.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-height-comparison"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-height-comparison</summary>

*Proof.* Decompose $\rho$ into a finite linear combination of differences of smooth unit masses. For a single such difference, sample its two endpoints independently at each of the two occurrences in the second moment. For a loop $L$, let $d_i^{\mathrm{geom}}(L)$ and $d_i^{\mathrm{cell}}(L)$ be its winding-indicator differences for the two height conventions at the $i$-th endpoint pair. Averaging the common fair signs gives the mixed second-moment integrand $$\mathbb E\sum_L
   \bigl(d_1^{\mathrm{geom}}(L)-d_1^{\mathrm{cell}}(L)\bigr)
   \bigl(d_2^{\mathrm{geom}}(L)-d_2^{\mathrm{cell}}(L)\bigr).$$ At a fixed tuple of four distinct endpoints, put $d_*>0$ for their minimum separation, truncated at one. A nonzero term requires the same loop to enter an $O(\delta)$ neighborhood of an endpoint of each pair. For small enough $\delta$ that loop has diameter at least $d_*/2$. The bulk one-arm estimate makes such a macroscopic loop’s approach to a mesh-sized endpoint neighborhood negligible. Higher passage-count moments give uniform integrability on each fixed size range; the arm bound for a loop visiting the bounded support and reaching a large radius removes the remaining tail. Thus this integrand tends to zero at every distinct endpoint tuple.

The octave passage-count bounds also give the integrable majorant $C(1+|\log(d_*\vee\delta)|)^2$. Indeed every contributing loop has size at least the endpoint separation up to a mesh error, the count has bounded moments per octave, and the outer octaves have a power-decaying tail. The same estimate holds for each of the four mixed terms in the displayed product. Dominated convergence in the independently sampled endpoints proves <a href="#q4field:height-comparison-L2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:height-comparison-L2">[q4field:height-comparison-L2]</a>; tuples with coincidences have zero integration measure. A finite linear decomposition and Cauchy–Schwarz give the assertion for $\rho$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4field-wholeplane-input"></a>
<div id="q4field:wholeplane-input" class="proposition">

**Proposition 73** (Whole-plane height convergence). *For every real $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb C)$ with $\int\rho=0$, the independent fair unit-jump height of critical square-lattice $\operatorname{FK}_4$ satisfies <a id="q4field:plane-characteristic"></a>$$\label{q4field:plane-characteristic}
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
 \mathbb E\exp\bigl(i\langle h_\delta,\rho\rangle\bigr)
 =\exp\left\{-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}
  \iint\rho(x)G_{\mathbb C}(x,y)\rho(y)\,dx\,dy\right\}.$$ The same assertion holds jointly for finitely many such tests.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-wholeplane-input"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-wholeplane-input</summary>

*Proof.* Corollary <a href="#cor:rr-gff-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:rr-gff-input">71</a> gives this statement for the cellwise height. Lemma <a href="#q4field:height-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:height-comparison">72</a> transfers it to the smoothed geometric height, since the difference of the characteristic functions is bounded by $\mathbb E|\langle h_\delta^{\mathrm{geom}}
-h_\delta^{\mathrm{cell}},\rho\rangle|$. Apply the same argument to every real linear combination of finitely many tests to obtain joint convergence. ◻

</details>

The parameters in Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Lammers, et al. (2026, Theorem 2.8 and Corollary 3.2) <a id="pm-cite-57"></a>[[SixVertexGFF2026](#ref-SixVertexGFF2026)] are $c=2$, $\Delta=-1$, and $\mu=0$. The loop factor is then an ordinary cosine, exactly the characteristic function of a fair sign multiplying a unit jump. The proposition concerns only the whole-plane field; finite-domain and conditional-field statements are proved below.

<a id="pm-h-98"></a>
#### Moments and binary transport

We first record why characteristic-function convergence supplies the moments used below. This argument uses only the bulk crossing theorem, which includes $q=4$ (Duminil-Copin, Li, and Manolescu 2018) <a id="pm-cite-58"></a>[[DCLM2019Isoradial](#ref-DCLM2019Isoradial)], and the actual-component counting argument of Section <a href="#sec:preliminaries" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:preliminaries">2</a>.

<a id="stmt-q4field-neutral-moments"></a>
<div id="q4field:neutral-moments" class="lemma">

**Lemma 74** (Neutral moment bounds). *For finitely many smooth compactly supported neutral densities, their height pairings have uniformly bounded moments of every fixed order. All their joint moments converge to the corresponding Gaussian moments. The bounds and limits are unchanged by the $O(\delta)$ drawing modifications just described.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-neutral-moments"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-neutral-moments</summary>

<a id="q4field:even-assignment"></a>
*Proof.* It suffices, by linear decomposition, to use differences of two smooth unit masses. Expand a product of $m$ such pairings, integrating the two endpoints of each occurrence separately. For fixed sampled endpoints $a_i,b_i$, put $$d_i(L)=\mathbf1_{\{a_i\in\operatorname{int}L\}}
       -\mathbf1_{\{b_i\in\operatorname{int}L\}}.$$ Conditional on the loops, averaging the fair signs gives exactly $$\label{q4field:even-assignment}
 \mathbb E_{\epsilon}\prod_{i=1}^m
       \sum_L\epsilon_Ld_i(L)
 =\sum_{f:\{1,\ldots,m\}\to\{\text{loops}\}}
       \prod_i d_i(f(i))
       \prod_L\mathbf1_{\{|f^{-1}(L)|\text{ is even}\}}.$$ In a nonzero term every used loop separates the endpoints in each slot assigned to it and is used in at least two slots. If $d_*$ is the smallest distance between the $2m$ sampled endpoints, truncated at $1$, such a loop has diameter at least $d_*$. Notice that even repeated copies of the same smeared charge have separately sampled endpoints; coincidences have zero integration measure.

For each endpoint and each size octave, the number of loops of that size which wind around it has moments of every order bounded uniformly in the mesh. Indeed such a loop supplies a passage in one of a bounded number of buffered annuli of comparable size. Ordering their medial passages produces distinct actual bank components, with bounded multiplicity. Successive actual-component exploration and bulk RSW give a geometric tail for this count. Between $d_*$ and the diameter of the fixed support there are $O(1+|\log d_*|)$ octaves. For larger loops, separation of two support points forces a visit to a fixed bounded slit joining them. Reaching the octave of radius $R$ then requires an actual arm from that bounded region to scale $R$, whose probability decays as a power of $R$. Cauchy–Schwarz and higher passage-count moments make the sum of these outer octaves finite. Consequently the absolute value of the integrand in <a href="#q4field:even-assignment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:even-assignment">[q4field:even-assignment]</a>, after expectation, is bounded by $$C_m\bigl(1+|\log(d_*\vee\delta)|\bigr)^m.$$ The same reasoning bounds any fixed higher absolute moment of the geometric majorant. Logarithmic singularities are locally integrable in the independently sampled endpoints. This proves uniform integrability of every fixed moment. Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a> and uniform integrability now give joint moment convergence.

If a drawing modification changes a contributing indicator at one of a fixed collection of distinct sampled endpoints, a loop of positive diameter enters an $O(\delta)$ neighborhood of that endpoint. The bulk one-arm estimate makes this event negligible; the preceding higher moment bounds allow its removal under the integrals. ◻

</details>

The binary index propagates by equality along every directed strand. At a tile, sum the two possible pairings with equal coefficient. An inserted matrix acts on this binary index, and a closed loop with ordered insertions $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ has conditional response $\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(M_1\cdots M_k)$. Thus the unperturbed loop weight is $\operatorname{tr}I=2$.

<a id="stmt-q4field-reflection"></a>
<div id="q4field:reflection" class="lemma">

**Lemma 75** (The reflected vacuum). *The plane binary-index network is reflection positive across the translated lattice symmetry lines parallel to either axis or to a diagonal. Reflection reverses directed transport and takes inserted matrices to their adjoints. Simultaneous conjugation by $SU(2)$ is unitary on the reflected Hilbert space.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-reflection"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-reflection</summary>

*Proof.* For a vertical cut through a primal column, a bisected tile contributes the seam operator $$I+|\mathrm{Bell}\rangle\langle\mathrm{Bell}|,
 \qquad \mathrm{Bell}=e_1\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_2,$$ which is positive. The horizontal case is identical. A diagonal cut along tile edges contracts equal indices, and is positive as well. These statements give a positive Gram form for arbitrary finite network replacements strictly on one side of the cut. Each switch intertwines the transports on its reference-directed pairs, so simultaneous conjugation preserves all contractions; reflection therefore implements it unitarily.

One may first use large reflection-periodic tori, with two reflection seams. For a diagonal seam take periods along and perpendicular to the diagonal. The all-loop torus measure differs from periodic FK by a bounded genus factor. A fixed patch is, with probability tending to one, screened by contractible actual circuits of both colors. On that event the genus data are exterior to the patch. Bulk uniqueness and the circuit tails identify every local subsequential limit with the plane FK state. Equivalently, finite closure of all strands meeting the patch gives its plane domain Markov law directly. Independent binary indices pass to this limit. The finite-volume positive forms therefore give the asserted plane form. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-99"></a>
#### From the spin-two sector to four arms

Write $\pi_4^\delta(r,R)$ for the plane probability of four alternating actual primal and dual arms across a square annulus. Fixed changes of its rims change this probability by at most constant factors. We use also separated prescribed landing sectors and their buffered extensions, at a bounded multiplicative cost. These are bulk statements at $p_c$; the published alternating-arm result includes $q=4$ (Duminil-Copin and Manolescu 2022, Proposition 2.3 and the arm-separation discussion) <a id="pm-cite-59"></a>[[DM2022Scaling](#ref-DM2022Scaling)]. No boundary RSW theorem at $q=4$ is used.

<a id="stmt-q4field-four-arm"></a>
<div id="q4field:four-arm" class="proposition">

<a id="q4field:four-arm-bound"></a>
**Proposition 76** (A bulk four-arm bound). *There is a constant $C$ such that, for $0<r<R$, $$\label{q4field:four-arm-bound}
 \limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\pi_4^\delta(r,R)
 \le C(r/R)^2.$$ The same bound, with a constant depending on the fixed bulk collar, holds inside a domain with arbitrary exterior boundary data.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-four-arm"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-four-arm</summary>

*Proof.* Scale the outer radius to a fixed small constant. Choose mirror boxes of radius $s$ at horizontal distance one, centered at $x$ and $y$. In the box at $x$, take a positive unit mass in a disk of radius $\varepsilon s$ at $x+(s/2,0)$ and a negative unit mass near $x-(s/2,0)$; use their reflected placement at $y$. Fix smooth mass profiles and connecting slits inside the boxes. Their height differences are denoted $h_x,h_y$.

<a id="q4field:spin-two"></a>
For a traceless complex $2\times2$ matrix $V$, insert $\exp(taV)$ along each successive directed flux piece, where $a$ is its contribution to this smeared dipole. Equivalently, if $\rho_x$ is the dipole density, choose a compactly supported one-form $\alpha_x$ in its box with $d\alpha_x=\rho_x\,dx\wedge dy$, and integrate $\alpha_x$ along the directed pieces. Such a form exists because $\int\rho_x=0$. Let $A(V)$ be the second-order coefficient as a vector in the reflected space. It is an equivariant quadratic map on the complexified conjugation representation of $SU(2)$. Its symmetric square decomposes into a scalar representation and one irreducible spin-two representation. Set $$E=e_1e_2^*,\qquad F=E^*,\qquad H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1).$$ The tensor $E\otimes E$ lies entirely in spin two, whereas the spin-two projection of $H\otimes H$ is nonzero. Unitary equivariance and irreducibility therefore give, with an absolute constant, $$\label{q4field:spin-two}
 \|A(E)\|^2
 \le C\left\|A(H)-\frac12\mathbb E(h_x^2)\mathbf1\right\|^2
 =\frac C4\operatorname{Cov}(h_x^2,h_y^2).$$ Here $\mathbf1$ is the vacuum vector. This does not assert that the entire scalar sector consists of multiples of $\mathbf1$: projection onto spin two annihilates $\mathbf1$, which is all the inequality requires. For diagonal $H$, the second coefficient is $h_x^2/2$, giving the last equality with the reflected orientation convention.

<a id="q4field:spin-upper"></a>
By Lemma <a href="#q4field:neutral-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:neutral-moments">74</a>, the covariance in <a href="#q4field:spin-two" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:spin-two">[q4field:spin-two]</a> converges to its Gaussian value. The covariance of the two neutral charges is $O(s^2)$, since the logarithmic kernel is smooth between the boxes and each charge has total mass zero and first absolute moment $O(s)$. The Gaussian identity $\operatorname{Cov}(X^2,Y^2)=2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2$ gives $$\label{q4field:spin-upper}
 \limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\|A(E)\|^2\le C_\varepsilon s^4.$$

<a id="q4field:coefficient-bound"></a>
We obtain a matching lower bound from two passages at each box. For a loop visiting both boxes, compress each maximal run at one box before its next visit to the other into one factor. Nilpotence gives alternating factors $$I+ta_1E,\ I+ub_1F,\ I+ta_2E,\ I+ub_2F,\ldots.$$ Close an excursion by an arc through the omitted other box, where the relevant one-form vanishes. The closing arc can be chosen disjoint from the excursion, giving a simple curve. Its flux is an averaged winding difference, so $|a_i|,|b_i|
\le1$. The fluxes are integers if the excursions avoid the endpoint supports. Let $M$ be the total number of alternating periods, over all loops visiting both boxes. There are $2M$ disjoint connecting passages. The coefficient $K$ of $t^2u^2$ in the product of normalized traces satisfies $$\label{q4field:coefficient-bound}
 |K|\le C M^4,\qquad K=0\quad\hbox{if }M<2.$$ Loops visiting only one box contribute $1$ and can be omitted.

If $M=2$ and the endpoint supports are missed, then $K\ge0$. For a single two-period loop its only possible nonzero contribution is $a_1a_2b_1b_2/2$. The full winding difference belongs to $\{-1,0,1\}$, so nonzero integer fluxes satisfy $a_1=-a_2$ and $b_1=-b_2$; the coefficient is $1/2$. For two one-period loops the coefficient is $a_1b_1a_2b_2/4$. If nonzero, both simple loops separate the two endpoint pairs. Their interiors are disjoint or nested, so their choices of the contained endpoints either agree in both boxes or are complementary in both. Hence the products $a_1b_1$ and $a_2b_2$ have the same sign, and this coefficient is $1/4$.

<a id="q4field:relative-tail"></a>
<a id="q4field:relative-hit"></a>
For completeness, the errors in this sign calculation must be *relative* to two four-arm probabilities. Let $\pi_4=\pi_4^\delta(c_1s,c_2)$, for fixed suitable constants. Bulk component searches give $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\bigl[M^4\mathbf1_{\{M\ge3\}}\bigr]
   &\le o_s(1)\pi_4^2,\label{q4field:relative-tail}\\
 \mathbb P(M=2,\text{ an endpoint support is hit})
   &\le C\varepsilon^\alpha\pi_4^2,\label{q4field:relative-hit}
\end{aligned}$$ for some $\alpha>0$, with the mesh taken sufficiently small at each fixed $s,\varepsilon$. Here is the exploration underlying these estimates. Around either box the $2M$ radial separators, cropped with end margins, give $2M$ alternating bank arms and at least $M$ distinct actual primal crossing components of a cropped annulus. Conversely, two distinct actual primal crossing components force two intervening dual separators, hence four alternating arms in a slightly narrower annulus. Thus the first two successful discoveries already cost $C\pi_4$. Expose each complete actual component, including all its exiting edges revealed closed, and do not count wire identifications as open paths. The remaining graph is dominated by the original annular lattice with maximal identifications at its original rims. In separated dyadic rings, a buffered dual circuit blocks every actual radial crossing with uniformly positive conditional probability. Each further discovered crossing therefore costs at most $Cs^\alpha$. Iterating this bound gives a summable tail even after multiplication by $M^4$. The two box annuli have disjoint bulk collars, so their first-four-arm costs multiply up to a constant; this proves <a href="#q4field:relative-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:relative-tail">[q4field:relative-tail]</a>. An endpoint hit additionally requires a bank arm from radius $\varepsilon s$ to a fixed small multiple of $s$, in a buffered region inside the hole of its corresponding four-arm annulus. Both four-arm costs are retained. The same conditional blocking estimate proves <a href="#q4field:relative-hit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:relative-hit">[q4field:relative-hit]</a>. In particular an absolute $o(1)$ bound would not suffice in either estimate.

Finally there is a compatible positive event of probability at least $c\pi_4^2$, with $c$ independent of sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Prescribe primal east/west and dual north/south landings at each box annulus, with buffered extensions. Attach the two primal inner landings to small actual circuits around the positive and negative endpoint disks, respectively, at radii $\eta s$, where the small constant $\eta>0$ is fixed before choosing $\varepsilon\ll\eta$. At the large scale join the inward primal arms directly between the boxes, and the outward pair around their exterior. Join the upper dual arms to each other and the lower dual arms to each other between these routes. At each inner rim join its two dual arms in a central corridor between the terminals. Together these dual connections form a closed oval separating the two primal groups. Retain one inner-to-outer landing pairing of comparable probability at the first annulus and its mirror at the second; the gluing works for either pairing. One of the two pairing classes has at least half the separated-arm probability, so no additional theorem concerning a prescribed pairing is needed.

<figure id="q4field:gluing-figure">

<figcaption>The bulk gluing used in the lower bound. Black connections join the positive terminals and the negative terminals separately; the dual oval keeps these two actual primal clusters distinct. Each terminal is protected by a small primal circuit. Only connectivity is depicted; the four-arm annuli are schematic.</figcaption>
</figure>

 \draw[very thick] (-1.65,0)--(1.65,0);

 \draw[blue!70!black,thick]

All these joins can be made in finitely many disjoint tubes of the requested colors, outside the core annuli except for their landing extensions. Use transverse crossings in overlap rectangles to join the extensions to the tubes. Condition on the complement of one color’s tubes and apply FKG and buffered RSW there, then do the other color. Since only that color’s extensions enter its tubes, the requirements are increasing in the appropriate conditional model. The two core annulus probabilities multiply by the bulk collar comparison. The resulting positive and negative terminal circuits belong to two distinct actual primal clusters, the first connecting the two positive terminals and the second the two negative ones.

There are at least two distinct closed interfaces separating these two connected primal groups: color parity makes their number even, and at least one is necessary. Each such interface separates both endpoint pairs and misses their support disks. On the part of this event with $M=2$, the two-loop coefficient is $1/4$. Subtracting <a href="#q4field:relative-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:relative-tail">[q4field:relative-tail]</a> and <a href="#q4field:relative-hit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:relative-hit">[q4field:relative-hit]</a>, first choose $\varepsilon>0$ small and fixed, and then $s$ small. Positivity on all the remaining $M=2$ configurations and <a href="#q4field:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:coefficient-bound">[q4field:coefficient-bound]</a> show $$\|A(E)\|^2=\mathbb E K\ge c'\pi_4^2.$$ Combining this with <a href="#q4field:spin-upper" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:spin-upper">[q4field:spin-upper]</a> proves $\limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\pi_4\le Cs^2$. Quasi-multiplicativity and fixed-factor rim changes give <a href="#q4field:four-arm-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:four-arm-bound">[q4field:four-arm-bound]</a>. Bulk collars give its domain version. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4field-contact-dimension"></a>
<div id="q4field:contact-dimension" class="corollary">

**Corollary 77** (Macroscopic contacts). *In any tight subsequential limit of actual loops or Dobrushin strands, the interior set of genuinely distinct visits by macroscopic curves has Hausdorff dimension at most zero, almost surely. Constant parametrization pauses are discarded. No assertion about boundary contacts is made here.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-contact-dimension"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-contact-dimension</summary>

*Proof.* Fix an interior compact set and an outer displacement cutoff $R>0$. A point with two genuinely distinct visits, each having displacement at least $R$, gives four medial passages across every sufficiently small surrounding annulus. With rim margins, their actual banks give four alternating arms. A grid cover at scale $r$ has $O(r^{-2})$ cells, each with limiting probability at most $C(r/R)^2$. Its expected number of required cells is therefore bounded uniformly in $r$, after the mesh limit. For every $\eta>0$ the expected $\eta$-dimensional covering content is $O(r^\eta)$; along dyadic scales it tends to zero almost surely. Countable compact sets, displacement cutoffs, and positive $\eta$ prove the claim. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:q4regular"></a>
### The field in regular domains

We now derive the finite-domain statement required for the loop identification. It is not part of Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a>.

<a id="pm-h-101"></a>
#### Actual walls and elementary bounds

Write $C\in\{\mathsf P,\mathsf D\}$ for a color and $C'$ for the other. An actual homogeneous wall is a simple polygon of $C$-diagonals, whose switches are forced open in color $C$. A mixed wall consists of an actual primal-diagonal arc, an actual dual-diagonal arc, and two tile sides joining their ends. Each tile side is a one-port transition gate. All interior switches not on a wall are sampled, including a switch whose diagonal endpoints happen both to lie on the wall.

<a id="stmt-q4field-wall-law"></a>
<div id="q4field:wall-law" class="lemma">

**Lemma 78** (Vacuum realization of a wall). *Conditioning the plane vacuum on exactly the stated wall switches gives the FK law inside with the indicated actual connections. For a closed $C$-wall, the $C'$ model on the strictly internal sites and its internal edges has free boundary condition. In a mixed wall, fixing the binary index at one transition port fixes the index of the distinguished strand; this condition has probability $1/2$ conditional on every switch configuration.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-wall-law"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-wall-law</summary>

*Proof.* An exterior connection of either color can enter only through the same-color wall arc, already connected by actual open edges. Hence it creates no additional interior partition. For a closed wall no $C'$ vertex is wired through that wall, giving the stated free model (equivalently, apply planar duality). There are exactly two transition ports in the mixed experiment. The loop through one must leave the interior through the other; its one independent fair index is fixed by the condition at the first port. ◻

</details>

<a id="q4field:domain-height"></a>
Set the height to zero on a homogeneous wall. In a mixed wall, take height zero on its primal arc and choose the distinguished index so that its dual arc has height one. Conditional on the geometry, $$\label{q4field:domain-height}
 h_\delta(z)=u_{*,\delta}(z)
      +\sum_{L\text{ internal}}\epsilon_L
                    \mathbf1_{\{z\in\operatorname{int}L\}},$$ where the signs are independent and fair. In the homogeneous case $u_{*,\delta}=0$; in the mixed case it is the $0/1$ side function of the distinguished strand. Values on the drawn curves are immaterial in integrals. For $f\in C_c^\infty$ in the interior, the pairing $\langle h_\delta,-\Delta f\rangle$ depends only on switches and binary indices near the support of $f$: integration by parts writes it as oriented flux against a compactly supported smooth one-form. It consequently does not depend on the relative height constant.

<a id="stmt-q4field-free-bank"></a>
<div id="q4field:free-bank" class="lemma">

**Lemma 79** (Free-bank estimates). *Consider a patch in which the bank color $C'$ has no forced open edge and no boundary identification on any domain wall meeting the patch. The graph may omit sites or edges. Counts of disjoint medial passages between buffered annular rims have moments of every order, uniformly in the mesh and in the remaining exterior data. The probability of an actual $C'$ arm across a ratio $R/r$ is at most $C_0(r/R)^\beta$ for some $\beta>0$. These statements hold as well for a product of free $C'$ models on disjoint subgraphs. In a bulk patch either color may be used.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-free-bank"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-free-bank</summary>

*Proof.* Order the medial radial separators and crop their actual $C'$ bank paths with margins at both ends. Different strips cannot communicate across a separator, and each strip is charged at most twice. Thus many passages force a proportional number of distinct actual crossing components of the cropped graph. Reveal these components successively from one rim, ignoring partition jumps. A deleted component does not wire surviving interior sites through its former neighbors. Since the wall is free for this color, the remaining graph is dominated by the full annular lattice with maximal ties only at its original rims. A buffered circuit of the other color blocks actual crossing, with conditional probability bounded below by bulk RSW. Iteration gives a geometric tail for the component count and hence all its polynomial moments. Applying these blockers in separated dyadic rings proves the power bound for one arm. Missing edges or sites only lower actual connectivity; the same comparison applies to a product on disjoint subgraphs. Enlarge inner radii by a fixed mesh multiple whenever needed. ◻

</details>

Take now a fixed simple rectilinear polygon $V$, with two distinct marked transition points on interiors of straight sides in the mixed case. Approximate it by the corresponding actual diagonal walls within $O(\delta)$, in marked boundary order. Such approximations exist: round each color arc on its own lattice and adjust its ends by $O(\delta)$ to join the two colors by a single tile side at each transition. This class of regular domains will suffice for the later comparison argument.

<a id="stmt-q4field-moment-kernels"></a>
<div id="q4field:moment-kernels" class="lemma">

<a id="q4field:log-kernel"></a>
**Lemma 80** (Moment kernels and compactness). *For the regular polygons just specified, the height moment kernels at distinct interior points $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ satisfy $$\label{q4field:log-kernel}
 \left|\mathbb E\prod_{i=1}^m h_\delta(z_i)\right|
 \le C_m\bigl(1+|\log(d_*\vee\delta)|\bigr)^m,
 \qquad d_*=1\wedge\min_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|,$$ with $d_*=1$ when $m=1$. Here $C_m$ depends on $V$ and $m$, uniformly over the interior tuples, including those approaching the boundary. Geometric majorants for the conditional signed expansions have higher polynomial moments with corresponding logarithmic bounds. Integrated moments are uniformly integrable; the height laws are tight as local distributions, and their moment kernels are asymptotically equicontinuous on compact sets of distinct interior tuples. The count bounds hold also for arbitrarily shaped homogeneous walls in a fixed bounded box and for products of disks of one wall color.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-moment-kernels"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-moment-kernels</summary>

*Proof.* A loop winding around $z$ and of diameter in $[r,2r]$ lies within $O(r)$ of $z$ and supplies a macroscopic passage in one of a bounded number of annuli of radius comparable with $r$. For a homogeneous wall use its free bank color. In a fixed mixed polygon, choose a subpassage away from the transition points by a fixed fraction of $r$. The two wall arcs separate linearly away from a transition, so the chosen patch avoids one of them and has a free bank color. Lemma <a href="#q4field:free-bank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:free-bank">79</a> gives bounded moments per octave. At mesh scale a deterministic local bound suffices. The same free bank argument works for arbitrary homogeneous wall shapes and for the stated products.

Expand <a href="#q4field:domain-height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:domain-height">[q4field:domain-height]</a> and average the signs. A loop which survives must be assigned to at least two of the distinct points and therefore has diameter at least $d_*$. The remaining offset factors have absolute value at most one. Minkowski’s inequality over $O(1+|\log(d_*\vee\delta)|)$ octaves gives <a href="#q4field:log-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:log-kernel">[q4field:log-kernel]</a> and the asserted higher moment majorants. Integrating the logarithmic singularities gives uniform integrability. Uniform second moments for compactly supported Fourier tests give tightness in a sufficiently weak local negative Sobolev space, hence tightness as distributions.

To move one point a small distance while the tuple stays distinct, any changed contributing loop indicator must belong to a loop of diameter bounded below which approaches that point. In the mixed case a changed offset requires the distinguished strand to approach it. The bulk one-arm estimate makes these events uniformly rare; the higher count moments control their contribution. This proves equicontinuity, allowing the $O(\delta)$ ambiguity of the drawing. The same annular passage counts give tight macroscopic curve counts and tightness modulo reparametrization by the displacement-arc subdivision argument of Section <a href="#sec:loops" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:loops">15</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-102"></a>
#### Neutral tests through a conditioned wall

<a id="stmt-q4field-regular-domain"></a>
<div id="q4field:regular-domain" class="theorem">

<a id="q4field:Q"></a>
**Theorem 81** (The regular-domain field). *Let $V$ be a fixed polygon and let its actual wall approximations be as above. Then $$\label{q4field:Q}
 h_\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ u+\sigma\Phi_V
 \qquad\text{as distributions in }V,$$ where $u=0$ for a homogeneous wall and $u$ is the harmonic extension of the boundary values $0,1$ for a mixed wall. All joint integrated moments converge. At every tuple of distinct fixed interior positions, the moment kernels converge to those of the same field.*

</div>

The proof has three parts. First we transfer local Laplacian tests through separated pieces of wall. Next we close the gaps between those pieces. Finally we determine the harmonic ambiguity left by the Laplacian tests.

<a id="stmt-q4field-analytic-displacement"></a>
<div id="q4field:analytic-displacement" class="lemma">

**Lemma 82** (Analytic displacement across a vacant slab). *Consider two groups of vacuum insertions supported in finitely many pairwise separated rectangles, with a vacant projection slab between the two groups. Its normal is parallel to a lattice axis or a diagonal. Normalize each wall constraint by the probability of its isolated switch constraints; allow bounded charge and index factors. Translate one whole group farther across the slab. Every subsequential continuum correlation is real analytic in the translation distance on a neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. This assertion also holds with other, previously fixed translations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-analytic-displacement"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-analytic-displacement</summary>

<a id="q4field:normalized-wall"></a>
*Proof.* First note the needed uniform norm bound. For a wall factor let $W_j$ denote its switch constraints only, and let $p_j$ be their isolated vacuum probability. Allowed lattice translations and reflections preserve $p_j$ exactly. The arbitrary-event comparison across vacant bulk collars gives $$\label{q4field:normalized-wall}
 c\le\mathbb E\prod_j\frac{\mathbf1_{W_j}}{p_j}\le C.$$ The constants may depend on the fixed gaps and rectangles. A single marked-port projection contributes exactly $1/2$ to the expectation of the positive wall constraints. Bounded charge or index factors can be omitted in absolute value. The same upper bound applies to separated subfamilies, their lattice translates, and their reflected copies. In particular the reflected norms needed below are bounded uniformly in the mesh. No lower bound on an individual, possibly very rare, wall probability $p_j$ is asserted.

On the algebraic reflected space let $S_\delta$ translate an insertion deeper into the half-plane by an admissible lattice period in the normal direction. Reflection and translation invariance make this operator symmetric. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$\|S_\delta^n v\|^2
       \le \|v\|\,\|S_\delta^{2n}v\|.$$ At fixed mesh every finite insertion is bounded, including its normalizing constants, so the norms on the right are bounded as the displacement varies. Iterating this inequality proves $\|S_\delta^n v\|\le\|v\|$. It also shows that null vectors remain null. Thus $S_\delta$ extends to a self-adjoint contraction on the reflected Hilbert space. Use $T_\delta=S_\delta^2$ to obtain a positive self-adjoint contraction. Write $p_\delta=O(\delta)$ for its physical translation step.

<a id="q4field:spectral-interpolation"></a>
Reserve a small fixed part of the vacant slab. After absorbing the rest into the positions of the two base vectors, the correlations have the spectral interpolation $$\label{q4field:spectral-interpolation}
 F_\delta(z)=
  \left\langle a_\delta,
    T_\delta^{N_\delta+z/p_\delta}b_\delta\right\rangle,
 \qquad N_\delta p_\delta\longrightarrow a>0.$$ The vector norms are bounded by <a href="#q4field:normalized-wall" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:normalized-wall">[q4field:normalized-wall]</a>. Spectral calculus therefore makes these a bounded holomorphic family on every closed half-plane strictly inside $\operatorname{Re}z>-a$. A bounded integer rounding of the exponent changes a correlation by $o(1)$ locally there: for $n$ of order $\delta^{-1}$ and bounded real $\theta$, $$\sup_{0\le t\le1}|t^{n+\theta}-t^n|=O(n^{-1}).$$ Thus rounding a physical shift by a bounded number of admissible normal translation periods gives the same limit. Take a diagonal subsequence on a countable array of rational shifts and apply normal-family compactness to <a href="#q4field:spectral-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:spectral-interpolation">[q4field:spectral-interpolation]</a>. Every resulting limit is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the entire nonnegative real ray, including zero. The assertion for one cut only uses the other translations as fixed parameters. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-q4field-neutral-removal"></a>
<div id="q4field:neutral-removal" class="lemma">

**Lemma 83** (Removal of a local neutral factor). *Let finitely many cells of one finite rectangular grid, separated by positive-width grid gaps, contain normalized wall factors, bounded index factors, and charge factors. Let one cell contain only $$X_\delta(f)=\exp\bigl(i\langle h_\delta,-\Delta f\rangle\bigr),
 \qquad f\in C_c^\infty(\text{cell};\mathbb R).$$ In the expectation of the product, this factor may be replaced with error $o(1)$ by <a id="q4field:neutral-mean"></a>$$\label{q4field:neutral-mean}
 \mu(f)=\exp\left(-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}
                            \int|\nabla f|^2\right).$$ The geometry and all gaps are fixed before $\delta\downarrow0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-neutral-removal"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-neutral-removal</summary>

*Proof.* Put $Y_\delta=X_\delta(f)-\mu(f)$. If an allowed reflection line separates this cell from all the others with a strict projection margin, reflection Cauchy–Schwarz proves the claim immediately. Indeed the squared norm of $Y_\delta$ tends to zero: the two reflected Laplacian tests have disjoint supports and their whole-plane Gaussian covariance is $$\sigma^2\int\nabla f\cdot\nabla(f\circ\theta)=0.$$ Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a> consequently factors their characteristic functions. Reflection conjugations and orientation signs do not change this conclusion. The other reflected vector has bounded norm by <a href="#q4field:normalized-wall" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:normalized-wall">[q4field:normalized-wall]</a>.

For general cell placements choose the original cells from a finite rectangular grid with positive gaps, and call the row and column of $Y_\delta$ its central row and column. The following finite displacement procedure creates the required separating line.

1.  Translate all rows above the central row upward, and all rows below it downward, each as a single group.

2.  Translate the columns to the right of the central column rightward, and those to the left leftward, by amounts larger than the preceding vertical spread.

3.  The central cell is now isolated in its $x+y$ projection. Partition all other cells into the groups with larger and smaller $x+y$ projections. Move these groups far in the directions $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$, respectively, until the former are above and to the right of all remaining cells and the latter below and to their left.

4.  Move the upper group farther right and the lower group farther downward. All other cells then have larger $x-y$ projection than the central cell.

Each movement begins with a vacant projection slab and increases its width. Individual rectangular collars stay vacant: each translated group moves rigidly, and the two groups at a cut only become farther apart. Each named directional movement is a separate one-parameter translation. Empty groups need no movement. The amounts are chosen successively sufficiently large, with each threshold allowed to depend on all earlier choices.

In the final configuration a diagonal reflection line separates $Y_\delta$, so every limiting correlation is zero. Apply Lemma <a href="#q4field:analytic-displacement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:analytic-displacement">82</a> to the last displacement. Analytic uniqueness extends the zero correlation from all sufficiently large values to zero. Continue in reverse order. At each stage the earlier parameters are still sufficiently large for the relevant vacant slab, and the later ones have been returned to zero. A countable set of rational choices suffices for a common subsequence. The triangular dependence of the thresholds therefore causes no loss of parameters. Eventually the correlation at the original placements is zero. Every subsequence has the same conclusion, proving the $o(1)$ assertion. ◻

</details>

We apply this lemma by cutting small positive-width gaps in the wall. Fix a tuple of interior positions and group its coincident positions. Choose a finite horizontal and vertical grid so that every group lies alone in an interior cell with strict margins. The grid lines miss all corners and transitions, and meet the relevant wall sides transversely. Remove the wall constraints in a thin strip at each such line. The remaining wall pieces have separated rectangular supports. The one marked-port projection, if present, belongs to one of those wall cells. In each interior cell combine all tests assigned to its group into one exponential. Formula <a href="#q4field:normalized-wall" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:normalized-wall">[q4field:normalized-wall]</a> bounds the normalizing expectation away from zero and infinity for this fixed gapped geometry. Successively applying Lemma <a href="#q4field:neutral-removal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:neutral-removal">83</a> identifies the joint Laplacian-test law under this gapped conditioning.

<a id="stmt-q4field-close-gaps"></a>
<div id="q4field:close-gaps" class="lemma">

**Lemma 84** (Closing homogeneous wall gaps). *For fixed interior charge supports and, when present, a marked port, the local normalized charge laws with gapped and complete walls become arbitrarily close as follows: first take the mesh limit at fixed positive gap widths, and then let those widths tend to zero.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-close-gaps"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-close-gaps</summary>

*Proof.* Consider one gap of width $\eta$ at a homogeneous wall point. The switches still to be fixed lie in a ball of radius $O(\eta)$, and are to be open in the wall color $C$. First omit the marked-index condition. In the opposite color $C'$, the gapped model is the larger of the two models. Couple by exploring all actual $C'$ components incident to the fixing edges in this larger sample, starting from both endpoints and revealing also all exiting edges. Use the ordered FK conditional probabilities for common queried edges. Explore actual open edges only, without following boundary partition identifications.

The only differing fixed data lie on the fixing edges. On the event that the discovered components stay inside a fixed small homogeneous neighborhood, their outside edges are closed in both samples. This screens the changes, so the unqueried graphs have identical induced laws and may be sampled identically. This is also a direct whole-plane exploration with only specified edge states; it requires no boundary wire jump. The probability that the exploration leaves the neighborhood is at most $C(\eta/R)^\beta$ by Lemma <a href="#q4field:free-bank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:free-bank">79</a>, where $R>0$ is its fixed radius.

Every discrepant switch is open for $C'$ in the larger sample, so both its $C'$ vertices belong to the discovered components. A loop or strand touching a discrepancy in either model has its actual $C'$ bank in those components. On the screening event it therefore cannot reach any charge support or the marked port, all outside the neighborhood. All remote loops and their binary indices can be matched exactly. Restoring the marked-index condition changes the exceptional probability by at most a factor two, since its conditional probability is exactly $1/2$. Repeat at the finitely many gaps and let their widths tend to zero after the mesh limit. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-103"></a>
#### Identification of the harmonic part

<details id="proof-stmt-q4field-close-gaps-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4field-close-gaps</summary>

<a id="q4field:laplacian-covariance"></a>
*Proof of Theorem <a href="#q4field:regular-domain" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:regular-domain">81</a>.* Take a subsequential distributional limit $h$, using Lemma <a href="#q4field:moment-kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:moment-kernels">80</a>. The preceding gap construction, Lemmas <a href="#q4field:neutral-removal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:neutral-removal">83</a> and <a href="#q4field:close-gaps" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:close-gaps">84</a> show that, in a neighborhood of every tuple of interior positions, the joint Laplacian tests have the Gaussian law with covariance $$\label{q4field:laplacian-covariance}
 \mathbb E\bigl[L(f)L(g)\bigr]
       =\sigma^2\int_V\nabla f\cdot\nabla g,
 \qquad L(f)=\langle h,-\Delta f\rangle.$$ For coincident positions all the tests are combined in their single vacant cell before applying the characteristic-function argument. This detail includes the diagonals of $V^m$ for every $m$.

More explicitly, the integrated moment bounds give moment distributions of every order for $h$, and hence for its Laplacian. On product neighborhoods of every position tuple they coincide with the Gaussian moment distributions just computed. Tensor test functions, partitions of unity, and their density in smooth compactly supported tests show equality on all of $V^m$. This excludes any unseen distribution supported on a coincidence diagonal. Every linear combination of finitely many $L(f)$ has the Gaussian moments; Gaussian moment determinacy identifies its law. Thus $L$ is a centered Gaussian isonormal field on $C_c^\infty(V)$ with <a href="#q4field:laplacian-covariance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:laplacian-covariance">[q4field:laplacian-covariance]</a>.

Extend $L$ by mean-square density to $H_0^1(V)$. For a smooth compactly supported density $g$, let $v_g\in H_0^1(V)$ solve $-\Delta v_g=g$ weakly, and set $$h^0(g)=L(v_g).$$ Then $h^0$ has the law of $\sigma\Phi_V$. For $f\in C_c^\infty(V)$, $v_{-\Delta f}=f$, so $\langle h-h^0,-\Delta f\rangle=0$. Consequently <a id="q4field:harmonic-ambiguity"></a>$$\label{q4field:harmonic-ambiguity}
 H=h-h^0-u$$ is distributionally harmonic, and therefore represented almost surely by a smooth harmonic function. No independence between $H$ and $h^0$ has been assumed or is needed.

<a id="q4field:boundary-kernel"></a>
It remains to show that $H=0$. We use moment kernels, not pointwise values of the limiting random distribution. Let $x,y$ approach distinct boundary points which are neither corners nor transitions. The uncentered second kernel of $h-u$ tends to zero. To see this before passing to the limit, use <a href="#q4field:domain-height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:domain-height">[q4field:domain-height]</a>. In the mixed case the wrong $0/1$ side at a point near its prescribed wall requires the marked strand to cross a short segment from that point to the wall. It must then leave a fixed local patch, since both marked ports are elsewhere. Likewise, a loop containing both $x$ and $y$ has diameter bounded below; a segment from $x$ to the nearby wall must cross it, so the loop approaches that wall point while leaving the patch. The free bank one-arm estimate makes both events rare. The uniform higher count moments in Lemma <a href="#q4field:moment-kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:moment-kernels">80</a> absorb their contributions. Finally the deterministic harmonic function $u$ tends to the prescribed boundary value. The homogeneous case has no marked term and is the same argument. Thus $$\label{q4field:boundary-kernel}
 K_{h-u}(x,y)\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{at distinct ordinary boundary points}.$$ Kernel convergence and equicontinuity on interior compact sets justify taking the mesh limit before this boundary limit.

<a id="q4field:angular-majorant"></a>
Let $\psi:\mathbb D\to V$ be conformal. Polygon corner behavior implies that $\psi$ and its inverse extend Hölder continuously to the boundary. In particular, for some $a,C>0$, $$|\psi(z)-\psi(w)|\ge C^{-1}|z-w|^a.$$ If $r,s\ge1/2$, then $|re^{i\theta}-se^{i\varphi}|\ge c|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\varphi}|$. The logarithmic second-kernel bound consequently gives an integrable majorant $$\label{q4field:angular-majorant}
 C\left(1+
    \bigl|\log|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\varphi}|\bigr|\right)^2$$ uniformly over radii approaching one. The same type of bound holds for the Dirichlet Green kernel, whose value tends to zero at two distinct boundary points.

Choose nonnegative smooth functions $\rho_t$ of integral one, each supported on a compact radial interval in $(0,1)$ whose two endpoints tend to one. For every integer $n$, consider the smooth distribution test which, for an ordinary function $v$, is $$B_{n,t}(v)=\int_0^1\rho_t(r)
       \frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}
       v(\psi(re^{i\theta}))e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta\,dr.$$ For distributions this is the pullback test; its density in $V$ includes the conformal change-of-variables Jacobian. It is smooth and compactly supported for each fixed $t$. Equations <a href="#q4field:boundary-kernel" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:boundary-kernel">[q4field:boundary-kernel]</a> and <a href="#q4field:angular-majorant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:angular-majorant">[q4field:angular-majorant]</a>, followed by dominated convergence in the two independent angles and radii, give $$B_{n,t}(h-u)\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in }L^2.$$ The Dirichlet kernel gives the same conclusion for $B_{n,t}(h^0)$. Hence $B_{n,t}(H)\to0$ in $L^2$.

The harmonic function $H\circ\psi$ has Fourier expansion with $n$-th circle coefficient $c_n r^{|n|}$. Therefore $$B_{n,t}(H)=c_n\int_0^1\rho_t(r)r^{|n|}\,dr
       \longrightarrow c_n.$$ All coefficients, including $c_0$, vanish almost surely. Thus $H=0$, and <a href="#q4field:Q" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4field:Q">[q4field:Q]</a> follows for every subsequential limit. Uniform integrability gives convergence of all integrated moments. The equicontinuity of the kernels at distinct interior tuples then upgrades their distributional convergence to pointwise convergence there, proving the last assertion of the theorem. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:q4rough"></a>
### The endpoint in rough domains

We work at $q=4$ throughout this section. We use the whole-plane height convergence of Proposition <a href="#q4field:wholeplane-input" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:wholeplane-input">73</a> and its regular-domain form, Theorem <a href="#q4field:regular-domain" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:regular-domain">81</a>. Write $$\sigma^2=\frac{2}{\pi},\qquad \lambda_0=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{8}},
 \qquad \sigma\lambda_0=\frac12.$$ The normalization of the Dirichlet Gaussian free field is $G_D=(-\Delta_D)^{-1}$, so its Green function has singularity $(2\pi)^{-1}\log(1/|z-w|)$. A signed height has an independent fair unit jump across each closed contour. Its offset is specified separately. Our purpose is to identify the conditional field in domains cut out by the contours themselves. Their boundaries need not be Jordan curves at this stage.

<a id="pm-h-105"></a>
#### Pockets and their conditional laws

A *wall of color $C$* means an actual connected open wall of that color, rather than an identification of separated vertices. Denote the other color by $C'$. All the following discrete drawings may be separated within a distance $O(\delta)$, where $\delta$ is the mesh, so that their contours are simple and have the prescribed traversal order.

<a id="stmt-q4pocket-discrete-pockets"></a>
<div id="q4pocket:discrete-pockets" class="lemma">

**Lemma 85** (Exterior-readable pockets). *In a homogeneous $C$-wall disk, each outer contour is the external perimeter of an outermost actual $C'$-cluster. Behind it lie pockets bounded by the maximal simple $C'$-open cycles, ordered by inclusion of their interiors. Their interiors are disjoint; several pockets can belong to one outer contour. The contours, these cycles, their assignment to contours, and all switches outside the pocket interiors can be determined without querying strictly interior switches. Conditional on these data, the pocket interiors have independent homogeneous $C'$-wall laws.*

*In a two-arc disk, first reveal the distinguished path. On either side, its bank together with that side’s wall arc determines analogous maximal-cycle pockets of the wall color. Conditional on the path and the exterior pocket data, all these pockets have independent homogeneous laws. A point wound by a containing contour or side closure, and farther than $O(\delta)$ from its bank walk, lies in one of the corresponding pockets. Every further contour winding that point is contained in that pocket.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4pocket-discrete-pockets"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4pocket-discrete-pockets</summary>

*Proof.* Draw each cluster as a small regular neighborhood of its actual graph. Its boundary follows the paired medial pieces within $O(\delta)$. Every perimeter behind its external perimeter lies in a bounded face of that graph. Such a face is enclosed by a simple cycle. Equivalently, the bank of the external perimeter is a closed graph walk; decomposing this walk into simple cycles shows that every wound point with the specified clearance belongs to a maximal cycle interior.

Two maximal cycle interiors cannot overlap without one containing the other. Otherwise their boundaries meet at two or more vertices, their union is contained in one biconnected block, and the simple outer boundary of that block encloses both. This contradicts maximality. Shared vertices or edges cause no difficulty, since the open interiors remain disjoint.

We justify the assertion about revealing information. Fix a possible list of cycles and expose its wall edges and everything outside its open disks. Any connection between vertices of one cycle that uses its interior already has a connection along that cycle. More strongly, adding arbitrary interior edges cannot join two distinct exterior biconnected blocks. After removal of an exterior cut vertex, the attachments belonging to any one wall cycle remain connected along the rest of that cycle. Thus an interior addition cannot repair an exterior cut vertex. The exterior block containing a maximal cycle already has all its vertices in that cycle’s closed disk: otherwise the simple external boundary of the block would be a larger cycle. A new cycle that both enters and leaves a listed disk would have two distinct wall attachments and would consequently belong to its wall block. It cannot enlarge that block outside the disk. The same argument applies if several listed disks are traversed, since they would then have to belong to the same exterior block. Nor can internal changes alter an external cluster perimeter. Consequently the event specifying the proposed list and its exterior is measurable from the revealed edges. Each wall is actually connected, so the domain Markov property gives the asserted product of homogeneous laws.

For the marked path, close each side using its wall arc and the appropriate half-sides of the terminal gates. The same-color bank and wall form a closed walk of actual open edges. The path lies outside every cycle made from this walk, so its exploration queries no switch strictly inside such a cycle. The preceding argument therefore applies on both sides. Finally, a further contour leaving a pocket and winding a point inside it would have to surround its wall cycle. This is impossible because that cycle belongs to an actual cluster connected to the original wall. ◻

</details>

For a family $\mathcal D$ of disjoint homogeneous disks, let $H_{\mathcal D}$ be the signed height with zero offset and independent laws in the disks. Its value at a point refers to the disk containing that point.

<a id="stmt-q4pocket-moment-comparison"></a>
<div id="q4pocket:moment-comparison" class="lemma">

<a id="q4pocket:moment-order"></a>
**Lemma 86** (Comparison of zero-offset moments). *Let $\mathcal D_-$ and $\mathcal D_+$ be two families of homogeneous discrete disks of the same wall color. Suppose that each disk of $\mathcal D_-$ is contained in a disk of $\mathcal D_+$. Assume all disks lie in a fixed bounded region. For distinct points $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ in the smaller interiors, $$\mathbb E\prod_{j=1}^m H_{\mathcal D_-}(z_j)
 \ \leq\
 \mathbb E\prod_{j=1}^m H_{\mathcal D_+}(z_j)+o(1).
 \label{q4pocket:moment-order}$$ The error tends to zero with the mesh, uniformly when the points have fixed positive pairwise separation. The statement compares moments, not signed heights in an ordered coupling.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4pocket-moment-comparison"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4pocket-moment-comparison</summary>

*Proof.* On graphs of the opposite color, the smaller laws are independent free random-cluster laws. Their product is stochastically dominated by the restriction of the larger laws: reveal the remaining edges and use the induced boundary partitions, which dominate free boundary conditions. Couple these opposite-color configurations by inclusion.

Consider a smaller outer contour that is relevant to the test points. Its cluster is included in a larger-model cluster, but the latter may itself be surrounded by a different cluster. Select the *outermost larger contour containing the filled hull* of the smaller cluster. One must make this selection even when the two clusters do not merge. Using nested regular neighborhoods of included graphs, or the cycle decomposition in Lemma <a href="#q4pocket:discrete-pockets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4pocket:discrete-pockets">85</a>, shows that this selected contour contains all the wound test points with clearance. Every relevant smaller maximal cycle lies in a maximal cycle behind the selected larger contour. In the surrounding case, the smaller cycle lies in a bounded face of the outer cluster and is therefore enclosed by one of its maximal cycles.

Retain only the two sets of exterior and pocket data from this coupling. Now resample their interiors using the conditional laws of Lemma <a href="#q4pocket:discrete-pockets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4pocket:discrete-pockets">85</a>. Their wall color has reversed, so the same free opposite-color comparison applies at the next stage. Iterate. This is a sequence of couplings of conditional marginals; it does not claim monotonicity of nesting depth in the original edgewise coupling. At every fixed number of stages it gives inclusion at the same numerical nesting levels. A smaller contour’s group of test points can merge with another such group, but cannot split. There is no extra contour of that level between a selected outer contour and a pocket behind it: the pocket wall is part of that very contour’s cluster.

To translate this construction into moments, expand each height as the sum of signs of its surrounding contours and average the signs. A term survives exactly when every assigned contour receives an even number of the indices $1,\ldots,m$. Encode that term by the vector of nesting levels $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m)$ assigned at the respective points. The same vector is admissible in the larger model: mergers add even multiplicities and hence preserve their parity. Distinct vectors remain distinct assignments. This is an injection between the terms counted by the two sign-averaged moments.

For a surviving term, each assigned contour winds at least two distinct test points and has diameter bounded below by their separation. All its ancestors have that lower bound as well. Truncate the number of such contours and ancestors. The free-bank arm bound makes the event that any of these contours passes within $O(\delta)$ of a test point negligible. On its complement all the required pocket containments hold. Lemma <a href="#q4field:free-bank" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:free-bank">79</a> and the higher count moments in Lemma <a href="#q4field:moment-kernels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:moment-kernels">80</a> remove the exceptional event and then the truncation by uniform integrability. This proves <a href="#q4pocket:moment-order" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4pocket:moment-order">[q4pocket:moment-order]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-106"></a>
#### Geometry before identification

The arm and passage estimates give three properties of every subsequential contour limit that we shall use. We spell out their endpoint content to avoid importing a crossing estimate at a true $q=4$ boundary.

<a id="stmt-q4pocket-geometry"></a>
<div id="q4pocket:geometry" class="lemma">

**Lemma 87** (Status disks and boundary traversal). *For every positive-diameter limiting contour, and for the limiting distinguished path, the set of distinct multiple visits in the original-domain interior has Hausdorff dimension at most zero. Deterministic interior points are almost surely avoided. At every interior trace point there are disks of each winding status arbitrarily nearby. In the marked case the statuses are read after closing the path on either wall arc. No nonconstant subtraversal of a limit lies entirely on the original Jordan boundary.*

*These statements and curve tightness hold both for the regular wall experiments and for the marked Jordan approximations in the theorem.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4pocket-geometry"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4pocket-geometry</summary>

*Proof.* The first two assertions follow from Proposition <a href="#q4field:four-arm" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:four-arm">76</a> and Corollary <a href="#q4field:contact-dimension" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4field:contact-dimension">77</a>, together with the one-arm estimate. For the two-status assertion use the attached-circuit argument of Section <a href="#sec:loops" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:loops">15</a>, with both banks retained. Here is the only modification required at $q=4$. Enlarge the first crossing band a little laterally, and give a label only to an actual component containing a crossing of the original core. After a component has been searched and removed, comparison with full wiring on the enlarged band’s boundary is still valid. A buffered opposite-color transversal extending past both lateral ends of the core blocks any further core crossing. Bulk RSW gives this blocker a uniformly positive probability. The number of labels is therefore tight, and each label represents an actual connection in the revealed past. The leftmost crossings from a label’s bottom sources in successive core slabs can now be used exactly as in the attached-circuit argument; the fresh-side circuits lie in interior balls. For a distinguished path, close it along the remote wall when reading the two statuses. The argument also works with exposed bulk data outside the test patch. Only buffered bulk RSW is used (Duminil-Copin, Li, and Manolescu 2018) <a id="pm-cite-60"></a>[[DCLM2019Isoradial](#ref-DCLM2019Isoradial)].

For the boundary assertion, fix a deterministic boundary point away from the marks. A macroscopic passage approaching it supplies an actual arm of the bank color that is not wired there. In local annuli this arm is bounded by the free-bank comparison. Along a primal wired arc the dual bank uses internal square faces and has no dual exit through that arc. Along the complementary arc the primal bank uses actual sampled edges and has no primal ties. Exterior dual identifications occur only beside the complementary arc. Turns can be followed by adjacent actual bank edges within $O(\delta)$. Any other induced ties in a buffered annulus away from the other arc attach the surviving graph only at its rims. Thus the same arm bound applies in the specified Jordan approximations.

A nonconstant boundary subtraversal would cover an arc and hit a point of a fixed countable dense subset away from the marks, by a macroscopic passage. The preceding bound excludes this. For tightness, at each displacement scale use a finite cover of subpassage tests away from the two marks. Every displacement contains a smaller displacement a fixed fraction of that scale away from both marks. Marked uniform Jordan convergence and separation of the two boundary arcs allow its annulus to be cropped in a neighborhood missing at least one arc. The same passage estimates apply there. Interior no-spur and multiple-visit tests always retain positive clearance from the original boundary. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-107"></a>
#### Protected cuts and pointed kernels

We next give the deterministic approximation needed for the conditional field. A single limit contour may have several open winding components; filling in its hull would incorrectly join some of them.

<a id="stmt-q4pocket-protected-cuts"></a>
<div id="q4pocket:protected-cuts" class="lemma">

**Lemma 88** (Outer comparisons with protected cuts). *Let $L_n$ be simple discrete contour closures in a bounded Jordan domain $V$, converging uniformly modulo reparametrization to $L$. The closures may include one original wall arc. Assume the geometric properties of Lemma <a href="#q4pocket:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="q4pocket:geometry">87</a>. Let $T$ be the trace of $L$, and let $U$ and $E$ be, respectively, the open sets of winding status one and zero off $T$, with infinity in $E$. Then the components of $U$ are simply connected pointed kernels of the interiors of $L_n$.*

*For every $\beta>0$ there exist simple regular comparison polygons $B_j$, and protecting balls centered on $T\cap V$ or $\partial V$, such that:*

1.  *the pointed kernels of $B_j$ at points of $U$ are precisely the separate components of $U$;*

2.  *every compact subset of $U$ is eventually contained in $B_j$;*

3.  *at each fixed $j$, deleting the part of a sufficiently fine discrete pocket outside $B_j$ changes edges only in finitely many protecting balls, of radii $r_i$, with $\sum_i r_i^\beta\longrightarrow0$ as $j\to\infty$;*

4.  *$B_j$ is connected to a region outside $\overline V$.*

*The finite protecting selection is made after constructing the cuts.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-q4pocket-protected-cuts"><summary>Proof of stmt-q4pocket-protected-cuts</summary>

<a id="q4pocket:exterior-closure"></a>
*Proof.* Every point of $T\cap V$ is approached by $E$, by the two-status property. Points of $T\cap\partial V$ are approached by the exterior of $\overline V$. Hence $$\overline E=\mathbb C\setminus U.
 \label{q4pocket:exterior-closure}$$ Compact subsets of $U$ persist in the approximating interiors by winding stability. Conversely, every excluded point is arbitrarily close to persistent exterior points, by <a href="#q4pocket:exterior-closure" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="q4pocket:exterior-closure">[q4pocket:exterior-closure]</a>. Thus the component containing a fixed point of $U$ is exactly its pointed kernel. Kernels of simply connected domains are simply connected.

Let $M\subset T\cap V$ be the distinct multiple-visit set, after constant pauses have been erased. Given $\eta>0$, cover *all* of $M$ by a countable collection of open balls $D_i$, centered on $M$, with $$\sum_i\operatorname{rad}(D_i)^\beta<\eta,
 \qquad \sup_i\operatorname{rad}(D_i)<\eta.$$ This is possible because $\dim_{\mathrm H}M\leq0$. Set $G=E\cup\bigcup_iD_i$.

We first show that any $x\in E\cap V$ can be joined to the exterior through $G$, after adding at most one arbitrarily small ball centered on $\partial V$. If the closure of the path component of $x$ in $G$ reaches $\partial V$, such a ball connects it to the Jordan exterior. Otherwise that component has a compact frontier $S\subset V\setminus G$ separating $x$ from infinity. The set $S$ meets $T$ only at unique-preimage points; its other points lie in $U$.

There are polygonal closed walks, arbitrarily close to $S$, of nonzero winding about $x$. To see this, grid the bounded component of $\mathbb C\setminus S$ containing $x$, retain its edge-adjacent squares reachable from $x$ without meeting $S$, and trace their external perimeter. We can lift these walks, with an error tending uniformly to zero, into the closed disks bounded by $L_n$. Near a point of $S\cap U$, a fixed interior ball persists.
